'''Don Lincoln''' (born 1964) is an American [[physicist]], author, host of the YouTube channel Fermilab, and science communicator. He conducts research in [[particle physics]] at [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]], and was an [[adjunct professor]] of physics at the [[University of Notre Dame]], although he is no longer affiliated with the university.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://physics.nd.edu/people/faculty/don-lincoln/|title=Don Lincoln|publisher=[[University of Notre Dame|University of Notre Dame Department of Physics]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150413210132/https://physics.nd.edu/people/faculty/don-lincoln/|archive-date=13 April 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> He received a Ph.D. in experimental particle physics from [[Rice University]] in 1994. In 1995, he was a co-discoverer of the [[top quark]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Abachi|first1=S.|s2cid=42826202|display-authors=etal|date=3 April 1995|title=Observation of the Top Quark|url=https://physics.columbia.edu/files/physics/content/pub_007.pdf|url-status=live|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=74|issue=14|pages=2632–2637|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.2632|pmid=10057979|arxiv=hep-ex/9503003|bibcode=1995PhRvL..74.2632A|hdl=1969.1/181526|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180621174208/https://physics.columbia.edu/files/physics/content/pub_007.pdf|archive-date=21 June 2018}}</ref> He has co-authored hundreds of research papers, and more recently, was a member of the team that discovered the [[Higgs boson]] in 2012.<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=The CMS Collaboration|author-link=Compact Muon Solenoid|display-authors=etal|year=2012|title=Observation of a new boson at a mass of 125 GeV with the CMS experiment at the LHC|url=https://physics.bu.edu/~tulika/Publications/Higgs-observation.pdf|url-status=live|journal=[[Physics Letters B]]|volume=716|issue=1|pages=30–61|arxiv=1207.7235|doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2012.08.021|bibcode=2012PhLB..716...30C|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190329214156/https://physics.bu.edu/~tulika/Publications/Higgs-observation.pdf|archive-date=29 March 2019}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Don Lincoln was born in 1964. He received a Ph.D. in experimental particle physics from Rice University in 1994.

== Research ==
Lincoln's research career began in 1987 as a graduate student using the [[Fermilab]] accelerator.  His thesis work used the highest energy photon beam to study the transition between nuclear physics and modern quark-based particle physics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.56.R5301|title=Emergence of jet dominance in photon-proton interactions}}</ref>  He then transitioned to studying high energy collisions between protons and antimatter protons using the [[DZero]] experiment at Fermilab.  In 2008, he began a transition to doing research using the [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] detector at [[CERN]].  During his research career, he has coauthored 2,000 publications.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/literature?sort=mostrecent&size=25&page=1&q=fin%20au%20lincoln%2Cd%20and%20tc%20p|title=Lincoln's publications|website=www.inspirehep.net}}</ref>  His expertise includes detector instrumentation, studying the strong nuclear force, and searches for new phenomena.

== Writing Career ==
Lincoln is a public speaker, science writer, and has contributed many scientific articles to magazines that include ''[[Analog Science Fiction and Fact]]'' in July 2009, ''[[Scientific American]]'' in November 2012, and July 2015,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/author/don-lincoln/|title=Stories by Don Lincoln|website=[[Scientific American]]}}</ref> and ''[[The Physics Teacher]]'' many times.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://scitation.aip.org/search;jsessionid=c4hfb37b0qbu.x-aip-live-03?value1=%22don+lincoln%22&option1=all&option912=resultCategory&value912=ResearchPublicationContent&operator8=AND&option8=pub_serialIdent&value8=aapt%2Fjournal%2Ftpt&qs=true&#93; |title=Advanced Search |access-date=2018-04-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161127103726/http://scitation.aip.org/search |archive-date=2016-11-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is also the author of books for the public about particle physics. His most recent book is 'Einstein's Unfinished Dream' <ref>{{cite book|title=Einstein's Unfinished Dream: Practical Progress Towards a Theory of Everything|last=Lincoln|first=Don|date=23 February 2023|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0197638033}}</ref> (2023)
and it is published by Oxford University Press.  His earlier books include 'Understanding the Universe: From Quarks to the Cosmos (Revised edition)'<ref>{{cite book|title=Understanding the Universe: From Quarks to the Cosmos|last=Lincoln|first=Don|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-4374-44-6|date=March 2012|edition=Revised}}</ref> (2012), 'The Quantum Frontier: The Large Hadron Collider'<ref>{{cite book|title=The Quantum Frontier: The Large Hadron Collider|url=https://archive.org/details/quantumfrontierl0000linc|url-access=registration|last=Lincoln|first=Don|date=4 February 2009|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=9780801891441}}</ref> (2009), and 'The Large Hadron Collider: The Extraordinary Story of the Higgs Boson and Other Things That Will Blow Your Mind'<ref>{{cite book|title=The Large Hadron Collider: The Extraordinary Story of the Higgs Boson and Other Stuff That Will Blow Your Mind|last=Lincoln|first=Don|date=21 August 2014|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=9781421413518}}</ref> (2014). In 2013, he released a book called 'Alien Universe: Extraterrestrials in our Minds and in the Cosmos',<ref>{{cite book|title=Alien Universe: Extraterrestrial Life in Our Minds and in the Cosmos|last=Lincoln|first=Don|date=9 September 2013|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=9781421424286}}</ref> which explains how the common images of extraterrestrials came to enter Western culture, and then goes on to explore what modern physics, chemistry, and biology can tell us about what real intelligent alien life might be like. He has been involved in a number of videos dedicated to disseminating discoveries in particle physics, and since July 7, 2011, has been a keynote speaker for a series produced by Fermilab that explores the range of issues dominating particle physics today in an accessible, and sometimes humorous way. Among the topics included in the series are the Higgs boson, [[antimatter]], the nature of [[neutrino]]s, the concepts of the [[Big Bang]], [[cosmic inflation]], the [[multiverse]], [[Leptogenesis (physics)|leptogenesis]], and [[supersymmetry]].<ref name="youtube.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLcrmvrXrZyHPifdqU1hjClY98HW7Lapk4|title=Don Lincoln Onscreen|publisher=[[Compact Muon Solenoid|USCMS]]|via=YouTube}}</ref>

His popularizations also include columns that translate CMS<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fnal.gov/pub/today/cms_resultofthemonth/index.html|title=Fermilab Today - Result of the Week Archive - 2013|website=www.fnal.gov}}</ref> (monthly) and DZero<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fnal.gov/pub/today/resultoftheweek/index.html|title=Fermilab Today - Result of the Week Archive - 2013|website=www.fnal.gov}}</ref> (biweekly) physics measurements for the public. He is also the author of a recurring segment, ''Physics in a Nutshell'', in the Fermilab online newspaper,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fnal.gov/pub/today/physics_in_a_nutshell/index.html|title=Fermilab Today - Physics in a Nutshell Archive - 2015|website=www.fnal.gov}}</ref> he blogs for the website of the television series ''[[Nova (American TV series)|NOVA]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/physics/blog/author/dlincoln/|title=Higgs and Englert Win Physics Nobel Prize|last=Lincoln|first=Don|date=8 October 2013|website=[[Nova (American TV series)|NOVA]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131025075556/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/physics/blog/author/dlincoln/|archive-date=25 October 2013|url-status=dead|access-date=26 August 2017}}</ref> and he writes for ''[[Live Science]]'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.livescience.com/topics/expert-voices-don-lincoln|title=Expert Voices - Don Lincoln|website=[[Live Science]]|date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180818052145/https://www.livescience.com/topics/expert-voices-don-lincoln|archive-date=18 August 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Big Think,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bigthink.com/people/don-lincoln/|title=Big Think}}</ref> and [[CNN]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://muckrack.com/don-lincoln|title=Journalism history |date=6 May 2025 }}</ref> Additionally, he has created over 100 videos that translate particle physics and cosmology for a lay audience.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCfRa7MXBEsoJuAM8s6D8oKDPyBepBosS|title=YouTube playlist|website=[[YouTube]] }}</ref> In collaboration with [[The Teaching Company]], he has released video courses that outlined the scientific community's modern understanding of a [[theory of everything]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thegreatcourses.com/courses/the-theory-of-everything-the-quest-to-explain-all-reality.html|title=The Theory of Everything: The Quest to Explain All Reality|website=English}}</ref> common misconceptions of science,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thegreatcourses.com/courses/understanding-the-misconceptions-of-science.html|title=Understanding the Misconceptions of Science|website=English}}</ref> and why scientists believe some of the mind-boggling claims of modern physics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thegreatcourses.com/courses/the-evidence-for-modern-physics-how-we-know-what-we-know|title=The Evidence for Modern Physics: How We Know What We Know|website=English}}</ref> 

== Honors ==
Lincoln is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2015&unit_id=FOEP&institution=Fermi+National+Accelerator+Laboratory|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=[[American Physical Society]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180121071425/https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2015&unit_id=FOEP&institution=Fermi+National+Accelerator+Laboratory|archive-date=21 January 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref>{{cite journal|date=25 November 2016|title=2016 AAAS Fellows approved by the AAAS Council|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=354|issue=6315|pages=981–984|doi=10.1126/science.354.6315.981|pmid=27885000|bibcode=2016Sci...354..981.|doi-access=free}}</ref> and recipient of the 2013 [[Outreach Prize of EPS|Outreach Prize]] of the High Energy and Particle Physics Division of the [[European Physical Society]]  “for communicating in multiple media the excitement of High Energy Physics to high-school students and teachers, and the public at large”.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/other-prize-awards.php|title=The Outreach Prizes|publisher=|archive-url=|archive-date=|url-status=|last=High Energy and Particle Physics Division of EPS}}</ref> He also was awarded the 2017 American Institute of Physics Gemant Award for "cultural, artistic or humanistic contributions to physics for achievements in communication and public outreach".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/news/2017/don-lincoln-wins-2017-gemant-award-aip|title=Don Lincoln Wins 2017 Gemant Award from AIP|date=12 April 2017|publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406040411/https://www.aip.org/news/2017/don-lincoln-wins-2017-gemant-award-aip|archive-date=6 April 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>  In 2024, he received the Klopsteg Memorial Lecture Award from the American Association of Physics Teachers for "passionate and profound career-long impact in sharing the excitement of contemporary physics topics in ways that interest and inform the general public about the relevance and importance of fundamental physics from cosmology to high energy particle physics through prolific and impactful communication and world-class public outreach programs.”<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aapt.org/aboutaapt/2024-Klopsteg-Memorial-Lecture-Awardee-is-Don-Lincoln.cfm|title=2024 Klopsteg Memorial Lecture Awardee is Don Lincoln|date=4 March 2024|publisher=[[American Association of Physics Teachers]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240423181647/https://www.aapt.org/aboutaapt/2024-Klopsteg-Memorial-Lecture-Awardee-is-Don-Lincoln.cfm|archive-date=23 April 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>  In 2024, he also received the Dwight Nicholson Medal for Outreach from the American Physical Society "for worldwide presentations and publications that educate students and general audiences on the meaning of fundamental scientific research."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/award/dwight-nicholson-medal|title=2024 Dwight Nicholson Medal for Outreach|date=15 October 2024|publisher=[[American Physical Society]]}}</ref>  Experimental collaborations of which he is a member have also received group awards, specifically from the European Physical Society HEPP (2013, shared by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations for the discovery of the Higgs boson)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://home.cern/news/news/cern/european-physical-society-honours-atlas-cms-and-lhcb/|title=2013 EPS HEPP Award|date=22 July 2013|publisher=[[European Physical Society]]}}</ref> and again (2019, shared by the CDF and DZero collaborations for the discovery of the top quark).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/PrizeAnnouncements/hep2019/EPS_HEPP2019_long.pdf|title=2019 EPS HEPP Award|date=31 July 2019|publisher=[[European Physical Society]]}}</ref> Most recently, he was a joint recipient of the 2025 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics (2025, shared by the ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb CERN experiments).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/91|title=2025 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics|date=5 April 2025|publisher=[[Breakthrough Prize]]}}</ref>
